children: Buck Mulligan is modelled after
Oliver St. John Gogarty
, a fellow Irish poet.
This opening scene is a parody of the
Catholic Mass

suggested here by the “stately” manner of Buck’s entry, which follows that of a priest or clergyman, and again with the “cross(ing)” of the mirror and the razor. The bowl in the scene, “held aloft” ceremoniously, stands in for the chalice of communion that contains the blood of Christ.
It’s significant that the first word of Joyce’s novel, ‘Stately’ contains its last, ‘Yes’. This is a story of return, and as we depart, we have the shadow of our destination in mind.

The yellow dressinggown: 16 June is the feast day of St. John Francis Regis (1597-1640), the appropriate vestments for a Mass would be white and gold. Within the church the colour yellow suggests degradation, jealousy, treason and deceit. As such Judas is often portrayed in a garment of yellow.
The ungirdled gown is in contrast of the priests vow of chastity and the “razor” refers to slaughter, with Mulligan, the priest, acting as a butcher.

By using the feminine “Christine” rather than “Christian” Mulligan is imputing a sexuality to the holy matter: Christ as woman. Femininity will play a role throughout the novel as the magnetic force behind Ulysses' journey in
Homer’s
Odyssey
as well as Bloom’s “search” for Molly. Joyce is planting metaphorical seeds that will bear fruit later. The careful reader can rejoice in these complexities with each additional reading.
As Mulligan holds aloft the chalice containing (or about to contain) God’s blood,
he acknowledges

that some of the flecks of shaving foam are experiencing difficulty in their effort to become “white corpuscles,” the antigen-destroying part of the holy substance. When medical students encounter miracles, they like to get their facts straight.

first canto

And lo! almost where the ascent began,
A panther light and swift exceedingly,
Which with a spotted skin was covered o'er!
And never moved she from before my face,
Nay, rather did impede so much my way,

(Longfellow trans.)

Although Longfellow translates “panther”, the animal mentioned here, “una lonza” is actually a leopard; throughout the first Canto Dante also encounters a lion and a she-wolf. Respectively, they are thought to be symbols of lust, pride and avarice.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Many folk suggest Dante’s Panther is an allegory for Florence and worldly pleasures, and Dante’s anger at their failure to revolt. Given Haines is English is this an allegory for Ireland-England relations and the Irish Rising?  He will shoot him if he doesn’t stop?
The ‘blacks’ are clarified below and the following note illustrates this sourced from
http://www.poetryintranslation.com/PITBR/Italian/DantnotesInf.htm#_Toc64100649
Salvation of Italy

There are various interpretations of Dante’s imagery, for example that the leopard (panther) represents Florence and worldly pleasure, lust or envy; the lion the Royal House of France, and ambition or pride; the she-wolf the Papacy, and avarice. Lust, pride and avarice are the three roots of sin. The imagery of the three animals may come from Jeremiah (v.6). The she-wolf, the Papacy, made many alliances.

The Greyhound (Veltro) has been suggested to be Can Grande della Scala, born in Verona, between Feltro in Venetia and Montefeltro in Romagna, the great Ghibelline leader. Dante’s later patron, he may have been regarded by Dante as the deliverer who would restore Imperial power, reinstitute Roman law, eliminate avarice, bring peace, and establish a reformed order of things.

Dante, whose father Aldighiero was a Guelf, and supporter of the papacy, traced his ancestry back to Cacciaguida, a crusader under Emperor Conrad III, and identified with the Romans who had allied Florence to Imperial Rome. He was of the populo vecchio, the populus, the old inhabitants, not the plebs, from Fiesole etc.  Dante’s opposition however to the dishonesty and corruption of the Papacy under Boniface VIII aligned him with the Ghibelline pro-Imperial cause, and opposed him to the pro-Papacy Guelfs. The Florentine families also split between the local Bianchi (white) and Neri (black) factions. Dante’s family belonged to the Bianchi. Ultimately the Bianchi combined with the old half-suppressed Ghibelline party, and the Neri aligned with the Papacy, claiming to represent the old Guelph traditions of Florence.

Dante’s personal ideals when fully developed were for an apolitical  Church, and an earthly Empire, both enfranchised by God, supreme in their own spheres, one of spiritual and the other temporal power. He was therefore opposed to the Guelf principles of his father (the Ultramontanism of Gregory VII and Innocent III), and to the democracy and plutocracy of Florence. He was equally opposed to the supremacy of State over Church asserted by the Emperors Henry IV and Frederick II, by Henry II of England, and Philip the Fair of France. Dante therefore found himself ‘a party of one’ caught in the cross-currents of his time, supporting an autocratic view of the Imperial State, and a desire for a reformed, spiritual Papacy.

An alternative candidate for ‘the Greyhound’ is Uguccione della Faggiuola, head of the Ghibelline forces at Lucca in 1315 when the Guelphs were driven out, and at the siege of Montecatini (within ten miles of Florence) where he gained a decisive victory. However Uguccione was eclipsed by 1316.

children: Referred to again soon after, this is Malachi’s wealthy and pious Aunt Ursula who disapproves of Stephen. Some researchers have identified this unseen character with Oliver St. John Gogarty’s real life aunt,
Anne “Annie” Henry Oliver

. Annie occasionally lived in the home of her sister Margaret Gogarty (née Oliver) and Margaret’s children, including Oliver St. John, after Margaret’s husband Henry died in 1891. She seemed to have played a role in managing the household and raising Margaret’s children, which matches the descriptions in this chapter of Mulligan’s aunt hiring the servants in his house, lending him money, and lecturing Mulligan about his company.

children: Dublin’s steam-powered
mailboats

ferried letters and packages from Ireland to Britain twice a day. This sighting helps time this moment to a few minutes after 8:15am. The mailboats also carried passengers between the two islands: in episode 12,
“Cyclops”
, we learn city councillor Joseph P. Nannetti is taking the evening mailboat to speak in Parliament the next day. This morning mailboat, some researchers hypothesize, may have been the source of the
“two strong shrill whistles”
that reply to Mulligan’s call at the start of the chapter.

children: The
sign of the cross

, a ubiquitous Roman Catholic gesture used to convey a blessing or a prayer of supplication, involves moving your right hand vertically then horizontally in a shape recalling the Cross of Jesus’s crucifixion. While clergy and laypeople alike often perform a solo gesture with hand close to their own chest and head, a Catholic priest may perform the gesture with their arm extended outward to “bless” another person in front of them, as Mulligan does to Stephen here as part of his mock priest shtick.
